title: Execution Control Harness for Governed LLM-Based Code Generation
journal: 2026 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
authors: M. Takeda and Y. Funaya and O. Harriet and R. Mibe and H. Kanuka
abstract: LLM-based coding agents have strong potential for automating software development, but their direct application remains fragile under long and complex requirements. Specification omissions are common, and autonomous local fixes can trigger cascading regressions. In a preliminary experiment, implementing a single business function using a standard specification-driven approach required 65 interaction rounds and approximately 9 hours of manual correction.In this paper, we propose an execution control harness that tightly couples LLM-based code generation with governed execution. Implemented as a YAML-based workflow DSL, the harness integrates mechanically scoped reasoning, deterministic validation gates, automated Git-based rollback, and hybrid human-agent control.A case study on a real-world insurance application of approximately 30 KLOC suggests that the proposed approach helps suppress specification omissions and regression chains. Under comparable conditions, the number of correction iterations was reduced from 65 to 3, and total development time decreased from 9.0 to 0.5 hours. These results indicate that reliable AI-driven software development requires not only capable agents but also execution control architectures that govern the generation process.

title: Spec-Driven AI: A Multiagent Framework for Specification-Centric SDLC Automation
journal: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
authors: J. C. Bello and D. Fazzioni and V. M. A. De Lima and T. N. Kudo and A. Da Silva Soares
abstract: AI coding assistants are transforming software development, but most approaches remain code-centric and weakly connected to requirements, specifications, architectural decisions, organizational standards, and quality gates. This paper presents Spec-Driven AI, a multiagent framework for specification-centric Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) automation. The framework combines an SDLC orchestrator, specialized lifecycle agents, human-in-the-loop gates, auditable artifact generation, and a Pattern Manager / Context Platform that provides governed context through repository indexing, document retrieval, knowledge graph extraction, adherence validation, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. Spec-Driven AI treats specifications as verifiable contracts and uses agents to coordinate discovery, specification, design, planning, implementation support, testing, review, and traceability. We describe the architecture, implementation, and demonstration scenario showing how a project is registered, indexed, governed, and used to prepare structured context for SDLC agents. title: Incentivizing Fairness in Autonomous Ecosystems
journal: 2024 50th Euromicro Conference on Software Engineering and Advanced Applications (SEAA)
authors: D. Halasz and D. Kusnirakova and S. Shandilya and B. Buhnova
abstract: In the realm of Autonomous Systems, the absence of direct human oversight introduces novel challenges as these systems start forming complex relationships. The emergent dynamics raise concerns regarding the fair distribution of resources and the promotion of altruistic behavior, which are traditionally moderated by human intervention. This paper envisions an innovative approach that integrates the monetization of acts of generosity in autonomous ecosystems to foster benevolent actions among autonomous agents and, therefore, promote the fairness of the ecosystem as a whole.

title: A Metadata-Driven Decision Framework for Open-Source Large Language Model Selection in Enterprise Deployments : A Use-Case-Weighted Evaluation Framework Grounded in Hugging Face Repository Metadata
journal: 2026 International Conference on Next-Gen Intelligent Computing and Applications (ICONICA)
abstract: The proliferation of open-source large language models (LLMs) on platforms such as Hugging Face has introduced a structural selection challenge for enterprise software teams. Existing decision frameworks for enterprise LLM adoption are qualitative and manual, while comparative performance studies lack a systematic methodology for identifying which specific opensource model to deploy for a given production context. This paper proposes a ten-parameter, use-case-weighted evaluation framework that produces a quantified fit score from repository metadata alone, without requiring direct model inference. The license parameter operates as a binary hard filter. The remaining nine parameters are scored on an ordinal rubric and combined through use-case-specific weights into a composite Fit Score, classifying models as Strong Fit, Conditional Fit, or Not Recommended. A set of use-case-specific veto rules enforces capability floors that override the composite score, ensuring that structural deficits cannot be offset by strength in unrelated parameters. The ten parameters identified are defined across three groups: (i) Trustworthiness, (ii) Technical Fit, and (iii) Enterprise Compliance, with parameter weights differentiated across three targeted deployment use cases: (i) Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), (ii) Code Generation, and (iii) Agentic Deployment. A model card completeness rubric with three classification tiers is introduced, including a use-case-aware reclassification rule that promotes benchmark documentation to a required component for Code Generation. The framework is demonstrated in a corpus that spans seven license types with parameter scales from 3.8B to 70B, producing meaningful, differentiated fit scores that reflect both usecase-specific capability requirements and enterprise compliance constraints, further identifying four conditions under which commercial models are preferable to open-source deployment. Since the framework scores repository metadata rather than model behaviour, fit scores express deployment readiness rather than measured task performance.

title: AgentLeak: A Benchmark for Internal-Channel Privacy Leakage in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
authors: F. E. Yagoubi and G. Badu-Marfo and R. A. Mallah
abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems create privacy risks that current output-only benchmarks cannot measure. When agents coordinate on tasks, sensitive data may pass through inter-agent messages, shared memory, and tool arguments, all pathways that final-output audits typically do not inspect. We introduce AgentLeak, a benchmark for evaluating internal-channel privacy leakage in multi-agent LLM systems. AgentLeak instruments seven privacy-relevant communication pathways and provides a large-scale empirical evaluation focused on final outputs, inter-agent messages, and shared memory. Across 1,000 scenarios spanning healthcare, finance, legal, and corporate domains, five production LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Mistral Large, and Llama 3.3 70B), and 4,979 validated execution traces, we find that multi-agent configurations reduce final-output leakage (C1: 27.2% vs 43.2% in single-agent mode) compared with single-agent baselines but introduce internal channels that raise total system exposure to 68.9% (aggregated across C1, C2, C5). Inter-agent messages (C2) leak at 68.8%, compared with 27.2% for final outputs (C1), meaning that output-only audits miss 41.7% of violations. Across all five models and four domains, the pattern C $2\geq $  C1 holds consistently. These results suggest, within the evaluated coordinator-worker setting, that privacy risk in multi-agent systems is strongly shaped by architectural coordination channels rather than final-output behavior alone: it arises from internal channels that remain invisible to standard output-level defenses.
